direct_answer: Ask your physiotherapist or local NHS musculoskeletal service whether aquatic physiotherapy is suitable and available. Some areas allow self-referral to physiotherapy, but hydrotherapy may need a separate clinical referral. Community pool sessions are not necessarily physiotherapy. Check water temperature, supervision, access, cost and medical screening with each provider before attending.

content:
Hydrotherapy, also called aquatic physiotherapy, uses exercises in warm water as part of rehabilitation. It may be an option when arthritis makes exercise on land difficult. It is not automatically the best treatment for every type of arthritis, and an ordinary swimming pool class is not the same as an individually assessed physiotherapy programme.

This guide explains how to ask about services and compare facilities. It is not a live directory or a promise that a particular pool has appointments. Local services, referral rules, opening times and charges can change.

What does NICE say about exercise in arthritis?

NICE NG226, recommendations 1.3.1 to 1.3.4, recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to people with osteoarthritis, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. It says to consider supervised exercise sessions. It does not specify a national hydrotherapy course length, waiting time or pool temperature.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE NG100, recommendation 1.8.1, says adults should have access to specialist physiotherapy with periodic review. This supports fitness, flexibility, strength and function; it is not a guarantee of hydrotherapy provision. Exercise is part of care and does not replace prescribed rheumatoid arthritis treatment.

How can warm-water exercise help?

Water's buoyancy supports some of your weight and can make movement more comfortable. Warm water can help muscles relax, and water resistance can be used for strengthening. NHS hydrotherapy services describe benefits for pain, movement and function. The amount of benefit varies, and warm water does not repair arthritis or remove the need for other care.

A physiotherapist can choose exercises, support and a level of effort that fit your joints and general health. The plan may include exercises on land as well as in water. Do not copy another person's pool programme or push through worsening symptoms because the water makes movement feel easier.

How do you ask for NHS hydrotherapy?

  1. Ask your current physiotherapist or rheumatology team whether aquatic physiotherapy would help your particular needs.
  2. If you do not have a physiotherapist, check your local NHS community musculoskeletal service or ask your GP practice how to access physiotherapy. The national NHS page explains that self-referral is available in many areas.
  3. Ask whether there is a hydrotherapy service, what its eligibility criteria are and who can refer you. Self-referral to physiotherapy does not necessarily mean you can self-refer to the pool.
  4. Confirm the current waiting time, assessment arrangements and number of sessions with the service. Do not assume a national timetable or guaranteed course.

For example, Royal Cornwall Hospitals says referrals must come through a physiotherapist and describes up to six sessions. NHS Lanarkshire's rheumatology service says people cannot self-refer to hydrotherapy and describes up to four sessions. Plymouth describes a course usually offering six to eight sessions at the physiotherapist's discretion. These are local examples, not UK-wide entitlements or a recommendation to travel to those services.

How do you find a community or private pool?

Look on your council or leisure provider's website for warm-water exercise, accessible swimming or hydrotherapy. Ask your physiotherapist whether they know suitable local options, especially if you are continuing exercises after an NHS course. A private physiotherapy clinic may also offer aquatic physiotherapy, but check what the service actually includes.

A warm pool session, aqua-aerobics class and aquatic physiotherapy appointment can have different supervision, exercise intensity and entry requirements. Do not assume a class is clinician-led because its name mentions therapy. Ask who runs it, whether they assess your health and what support is available if you struggle in the water.

What should you check before choosing a pool?

  • Suitability: is this individually assessed physiotherapy, an exercise class or an independent swimming session?
  • Temperature and depth: ask for the actual figures and whether they suit your programme. NHS examples vary: Royal Cornwall describes 34 to 35.5 degrees Celsius, while University Hospitals Dorset describes 35 to 36 degrees Celsius.
  • Getting in and out: ask about steps, rails, a ramp or hoist, changing facilities and help on the poolside. Check any hoist or equipment limits. Do not assume every pool has the equipment you need.
  • Supervision: who is in the water, who is watching from the side and what help can they provide?
  • Practical details: confirm current opening times, session length, booking and cancellation rules, charges, concessions and travel arrangements directly.

You do not necessarily need to be able to swim for assessed hydrotherapy. Several NHS services explicitly accept non-swimmers, but staff still need to check water confidence, depth and support needs. Tell them if you are anxious, cannot stand independently or need help changing. Acceptance at one pool does not prove that another can safely accommodate you.

Who needs a safety check before hydrotherapy?

NHS services assess medical history before pool treatment. Tell the team about heart or breathing conditions, breathlessness when lying down, recent surgery, a clot or cardiovascular event, epilepsy or blackouts, diabetes, pregnancy, continence needs, skin problems, wounds, infections and any other health changes. This is not a complete screening list.

Do not attend while unwell without checking with the team. New wounds, fever, infection, vomiting or diarrhoea may mean postponing treatment. Follow the service's own return-to-pool advice: published NHS policies differ, particularly after diarrhoea. Do not treat one hospital's time limit as a rule for every pool.

Some unstable heart or breathing conditions make pool exercise unsuitable. A familiar diagnosis is not an automatic ban either: the team needs to assess the condition and the setting. After an operation, follow your surgical team's wound-healing and rehabilitation advice before entering any pool.

What happens during and after a session?

After assessment, you may practise exercises with staff in an individual or group setting. Ask how long you will spend in the water and what to bring. Wear suitable pool clothing, bring a towel and ask how to manage drinking water, lockers and mobility aids. Poolside floors may be wet; use the agreed support and ask for help.

Tell staff immediately if you feel faint, dizzy or unwell, or develop chest pain. Stop the exercise rather than trying to finish the session. Warm water and exercise can leave you tired, so allow time to recover and discuss troublesome or persistent symptoms with your team.

There is no universal two-hour pain rule or fixed week when hydrotherapy must work. Agree goals such as walking, getting dressed or managing stairs, and review whether the programme helps. Reduce or stop an exercise that clearly aggravates symptoms and seek advice about adapting it. Ask for a plan for continuing suitable activity when the course ends.

When do symptoms need urgent help?

A suddenly hot, swollen and severely painful joint needs urgent GP or NHS 111 assessment, even without a fever. Do not enter a pool to see whether warmth settles it. Get urgent advice if you cannot move a joint or put weight on it, or symptoms are severe or rapidly worsening.

Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, collapse or chest pain that could be a heart attack. This guide is general educational information, not a diagnosis or a personal treatment plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can I self-refer to NHS hydrotherapy?

Local rules differ. Many areas allow self-referral to community physiotherapy, but hydrotherapy may require a separate referral and assessment. Check the pool service rather than assuming the same route applies.

How many NHS hydrotherapy sessions will I get?

There is no UK-wide number. Local NHS examples range from up to four sessions to courses usually offering six to eight, with the plan depending on the service and your assessment. Confirm current arrangements directly.

Do I need to be able to swim?

Not necessarily for assessed hydrotherapy. Tell the team about your confidence, mobility and support needs so they can decide whether their pool and programme are suitable. An independent swim session has different requirements.

Is any warm swimming pool the same as hydrotherapy?

No. Temperature alone does not make a session physiotherapy. Check whether there is clinical assessment, a tailored exercise plan, suitable access and the supervision you need.
